title: Leading the Difficult People in Your Church
subtitle: How a pastor handles the antagonist, the chronic critic, and the controlling personality without becoming bitter, where to draw the line between difficult and dangerous, and how to protect the flock from the few who would harm it.

sections.title: Every Church Has Them
sections.body:
No one warned me in seminary that a meaningful percentage of my ministry would be spent on a small number of people who made everything harder. They told me about preaching and counseling and the sacraments. They did not tell me about the man who has destroyed three pastors before me and intends to make it four.

Every church has difficult people. This is not a sign of a bad church. It is a sign of a church full of human beings, and you are one of them. Before we go further, say that part out loud. Somewhere in this congregation is a pastor who is difficult to be led by, and there is a real chance it is the one reading this. The critic in the third pew did not invent the category. He just occupies it more obviously than you do.

Paul named names. Alexander the coppersmith did me great harm. Demas, in love with this present world, has deserted me. Diotrephes, who loves to be first, will have nothing to do with us. The New Testament is not a stained glass world where everyone is kind. It is a record of real ministry among real people, some of whom were a genuine grief.

You are going to lead difficult people. The only question is whether it will make you wise or make you bitter.

sections.title: The One Who Is Never Pleased
sections.body:
The chronic critic is the most common difficult person, and the most exhausting, because nothing is ever quite right and you can feel yourself shrinking to manage him.

Start by separating two things you keep collapsing into one. Some critics are gifts. They see real problems and say what others only think, and a wise leader learns to mine the painful word for the kernel of truth it carries. The wounds of a friend are faithful. Do not waste a true criticism because the delivery stung. But the chronic critic is different. He is not pointing at a problem. He is feeding on a posture. The complaint changes; the discontent never does. Fix the thing he named and he simply finds another, because the naming is the point and the church is only his occasion for it.

With the chronic critic, stop trying to satisfy him. You cannot. His dissatisfaction is not about you and will not be cured by you. Receive him kindly, weigh his words honestly, refuse to be ruled by his moods, and decline to spend the ministry's emotional savings chasing an approval he is constitutionally unable to give.

The goal with a chronic critic is not to win him. It is to stay free of him while still loving him, which is harder and more Christlike than either capitulation or war.

sections.title: The One Who Must Run It
sections.body:
The controlling personality is a different animal, and often a more dangerous one, because he frequently comes wrapped in service. He volunteers for everything, gives generously, shows up first and leaves last, and slowly accumulates the kind of informal power that no vote ever granted him.

Then one day you make a decision he did not bless, and the warmth turns to ice, and you discover that all that service came with an invoice. The giving was a down payment on control. He did not serve the church. He purchased it, one casserole and one check at a time, and now he has come to collect.

The controller cannot be managed by appeasement, because every concession confirms his strategy and enlarges his appetite. He has to be met with steady, unanxious clarity about who actually leads. This is where many pastors fail, because confronting the controller means risking the money, the labor, and the relationship all at once, and the cowardly path of accommodation is always available and always self-justifying.

Diotrephes loved to be first and put people out of the church who crossed him, and the aged apostle John did not flatter him into cooperation. He said plainly, I will call attention to what he is doing. The church is not yours to control and not the controller's either. It belongs to Christ, and a shepherd who lets one strong personality run the flock has abandoned the flock to a wolf in a deacon's coat.

sections.title: Difficult Is Not the Same as Dangerous
sections.body:
Here is a distinction that will save you years of misery and possibly your church. There is a line between difficult and dangerous, and you must learn to see it, because they require completely different responses.

Difficult people are a burden to be borne. They are prickly, demanding, draining, and they are still members of the body Christ died for. You lead them with patience, you set boundaries, you keep loving them, and you carry the weight as part of the cost of shepherding sinners, which is the only kind of person available to shepherd.

Dangerous people are a threat to be confronted. The slanderer who divides, the predator who targets the vulnerable, the wolf who comes to scatter the sheep. These are not difficult personalities to be patiently endured. They are dangers to be named and resisted, and treating them like merely difficult people is not grace. It is negligence. Watch over the flock, Paul told the Ephesian elders, because savage wolves will come in among you and not spare it. He did not say be patient with the wolves. He said guard.

The pastor who cannot tell the difference either crushes the merely difficult as if they were wolves, or coddles the actual wolves as if they were merely difficult. Both failures destroy churches. Learn the line.

sections.title: Do Not Let Them Make You Like Them
sections.body:
The deepest danger in leading difficult people is not what they do to your church. It is what they do to you.

A few hard people, given enough room in your mind, will rewire you. You start preparing every decision against their imagined objection. You start reading your whole congregation through the lens of your worst three relationships. You become guarded, defensive, calculating, quietly cynical about the very people you were called to love. They did not split your church. They did something worse. They turned the shepherd into someone the sheep can feel pulling away.

Guard your heart, the Proverb says, for from it flow the springs of life. The difficult people will be in your church for years. Some of them will outlast your patience and outlive your tenure. You cannot always control whether they stay. You can control whether you let them take your softness, your hope, your capacity to be surprised by grace.

Lead them. Bear them. Confront the dangerous ones and refuse the bitterness the others offer you free of charge every single week. Because the day you become hard to protect yourself from hard people, they have won the only victory that actually matters, and the flock will know it before you do.
